intro: Most people never see a big game in person. They hear it, watch it or catch a short clip of it. In 1921 a Pittsburgh radio station carried a baseball game for the first time. By 1960 almost nine in ten American homes had a television. By 1979 a cable channel showed highlights all day and night. Each new way of sending a game changed who could follow it and what they remembered.

Records work the same way. A record looks like a plain number, such as 60 home runs or 8.90 meters. Behind every number sit choices: how the time was measured, how strong the wind was, what equipment was allowed, which drugs were tested for and which athletes were allowed to compete at all.

In this unit you will trace sport from the telegraph wire to the replay booth. You will read laws, rule books and rulings about records. You will be able to explain how media shaped memory and why a record can be an argument, and you will support your answer with dates and documents.
bigQuestion: How do the ways we send and count a game shape what we remember and what we believe is the best ever?

title: Numbers and Squares

chapters.title: Radio, Television, the Clip
chapters.bigQuestion: How did radio, television and the short highlight change what people know and remember about a game?

story.title: Ten Seconds from Three Hours
story.kicker: On October 3, 1951, a whole season came down to one swing, and one swing is mostly what people kept.
paragraphs: It is the afternoon of October 3, 1951, at the Polo Grounds in New York. The New York Giants and the Brooklyn Dodgers are playing the last game of a playoff for the National League pennant. In mid-August the Giants had trailed the Dodgers by 13 and a half games. They caught up in the last weeks of the season.

The Dodgers lead 4 to 1 going into the bottom of the ninth inning. The Giants score once. Then Bobby Thomson hits a home run to left field, and the Giants win 5 to 4. On the radio, Giants announcer Russ Hodges shouts again and again that the Giants have won the pennant.

The game is also carried on television across the country, one of the first sports events seen live from coast to coast. Yet the part that lasts is short. A recording of Hodges's radio call, made by a listener at home, is played for decades. Newspapers name the swing "the shot heard round the world."

Most people who later hear the call know nothing of the first eight innings. They do not know the score was 4 to 1, or who pitched, or how the Giants closed the gap in August and September. A game of close to three hours lives on as about ten seconds of sound.
story.think: What do you lose when a whole season is remembered through one short recording?

lessons.title: Scores by Telegraph
lessons.mainIdea: Before radio, the telegraph sent games out as short coded messages, and announcers later rebuilt games on the air from those messages.
reading: In the late 1800s most fans followed a distant game through the *telegraph*, a machine that sent coded messages over wires. Western Union operators at ballparks tapped out each play. Newspapers posted the results on boards outside their offices, and crowds stood in the street to read them inning by inning.

Radio stations later used the same wires. An announcer in a studio read a short telegraph message, such as a batter's name and the result, and then described the play as if he could see it. This was called a *re-creation*. Sound effects, like a pencil tapping wood for the crack of a bat, filled the gaps.

The best-known example came from Iowa in the 1930s. At station WHO in Des Moines, a young announcer named Ronald Reagan re-created Chicago Cubs games from telegraph reports. Decades later he became president of the United States. Re-creations lasted into the 1950s for some road games, because sending an announcer to travel cost more than a wire.

words.d: a machine that sent coded messages over electric wires, used for news and scores in the 1800s
a radio broadcast in which an announcer described a distant game from short telegraph reports
the largest American telegraph company, which sent game reports from ballparks

look.title: A Studio in Des Moines
look.text: A message arrives on a strip of paper: the batter's name and the words "flied to left." The announcer has no picture of the park. He tells listeners about the wind, the crowd and a long run by the left fielder. None of those details were on the paper.
look.prompt: Which parts of this broadcast were facts from the wire, and which parts did the announcer add? Why might listeners not know the difference?

check.q: What was a radio re-creation?
choices: A broadcast built from telegraph reports of a distant game
A newspaper story written after a game
A film of a game shown in a theater
check.why: Announcers read short telegraph messages and described the plays as if they were watching.

check.q: Who re-created Chicago Cubs games at WHO in Des Moines in the 1930s?
check.why: Ronald Reagan, later president, re-created Cubs games from telegraph reports at WHO.

check.q: Why did some stations keep using re-creations into the 1950s?
choices: Radio could not carry live sound
A wire cost less than sending an announcer on the road
check.why: Sending an announcer to every road game cost more than buying the telegraph report.

lessons.title: Baseball's First Broadcasts, 1921
lessons.mainIdea: In 1921 a Pittsburgh station carried a major league game on radio, and the World Series reached radio the same year.
reading: Commercial radio was new in 1921. On August 5 of that year, station KDKA in Pittsburgh carried a game between the Pittsburgh Pirates and the Philadelphia Phillies at Forbes Field. The announcer was Harold Arlin, a young worker at the Westinghouse company that owned the station. It is usually named as the first major league game on radio.

Arlin sat in the stands with a telephone-style microphone. He later said he was not sure anyone was listening. Few homes owned a receiver yet. Many early listeners built their own sets from kits or heard broadcasts in stores and clubs that owned one.

That October the World Series between the New York Giants and the New York Yankees also went out over radio. Reports were relayed from the ballpark to stations in the New York area. Within a few years, the World Series was a yearly national *broadcast*, and the *announcer* became a voice fans knew as well as the players.

words.d: a program sent out by radio or television to anyone with a receiver
the person who describes a game to listeners or viewers
a Pittsburgh radio station, one of the first commercial stations in the United States

look.title: Who Heard the First Game?
look.text: Pittsburgh, August 1921. A few hundred homes nearby have homemade radio sets. A shop on a busy street has one receiver turned up loud, and people stop on the sidewalk. Inside Forbes Field, thousands of fans watch the same game in person.
look.prompt: In 1921, which group was larger: people watching at the park or people listening on radio? What would have to change for that to flip?

check.q: Which station carried a Pirates–Phillies game on August 5, 1921?
check.why: KDKA, owned by Westinghouse, carried the game from Forbes Field.

check.q: Why did few people hear the first radio games?
choices: The games were played at night
Few homes owned a radio receiver yet
check.why: Radio was new in 1921, and most homes did not yet have a receiver.

check.q: Which event also went out on radio in October 1921?
check.why: The 1921 World Series between the Giants and Yankees was relayed to New York-area stations.

lessons.title: Chicago Opens the Airwaves
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's Cubs let many stations carry their games in the 1920s, while New York's teams later tried a radio ban.
reading: In the 1920s many club owners feared radio. They thought fans who could hear a game for free would stop buying tickets. Chicago Cubs owner William Wrigley Jr. took the opposite view. He let several Chicago stations carry Cubs games at the same time, and he did not charge them a *rights fee*.

WGN radio, owned by the Chicago Tribune, began carrying Cubs games in the mid-1920s. Wrigley believed radio would make new fans, especially women and children at home in the afternoon. Attendance at Wrigley Field rose in the late 1920s, and other clubs took notice of the Cubs' results.

New York went the other way. From 1934 through 1938, the Yankees, Giants and Dodgers agreed not to broadcast their home games. In 1939 the new Dodgers leader, Larry MacPhail, broke the *radio ban*. He hired Red Barber, an announcer he had brought to fame in Cincinnati, to call Dodgers games on the air.

words.d: money a station pays a team or league for permission to broadcast its games
an agreement among teams not to let their games be broadcast
the number of people who come in person to a game

look.title: Two Owners, One Question
look.text: Owner A says: "If fans can hear the game at home for nothing, they will not pay to come to the park." Owner B says: "A boy who hears the game on the radio today will buy a ticket when he grows up."
look.prompt: Which owner matches William Wrigley Jr., and which matches the New York clubs from 1934 to 1938? What evidence from the reading supports each side?

check.q: How did William Wrigley Jr. handle radio in the 1920s?
choices: He let several stations carry Cubs games without a fee
He banned all broadcasts from Wrigley Field
He sold the rights to one New York network
He allowed only road games on the air
check.why: Wrigley let many Chicago stations carry Cubs games and did not charge a rights fee.

check.q: Which three clubs kept their home games off radio from 1934 through 1938?
check.why: The three New York clubs agreed to the radio ban until the Dodgers broke it in 1939.

check.q: Who broke the New York radio ban in 1939?
check.why: Larry MacPhail of the Dodgers broke the ban and hired Red Barber to call games.

lessons.title: Networks Make a National Game
lessons.mainIdea: Radio networks linked stations across the country, so one announcer could reach the whole nation at once.
reading: A *network* is a group of stations that carry the same program at the same time, linked by telephone lines. The National Broadcasting Company, NBC, began as a network in 1926. Before networks, a game reached only listeners near one station's own tower.

On January 1, 1927, NBC carried the Rose Bowl football game from Pasadena, California. It is often named as the first sports event broadcast from coast to coast. A college game in California could now be heard live in Illinois and New York on the same afternoon.

Graham McNamee, an NBC announcer, called World Series games through much of the 1920s. Critics complained that he talked more about the crowd and the weather than about the plays. Listeners loved him anyway. His fame showed that the voice describing a game could become part of the *product* that stations sold to sponsors.

words.d: a group of stations linked together to carry the same program at the same time
a company that pays for a broadcast so it can advertise during it
something made to be sold; in broadcasting, the program that stations sell to advertisers

look.title: One Game, Many Towers
look.text: Picture a map of the United States in 1927. Dozens of radio towers dot the map, from New York to Chicago to California. Telephone lines run between them. On New Year's Day, every tower on the line plays the same football game from Pasadena.
look.prompt: How does a network change who counts as the audience for a single game?

check.q: What is a radio network?
choices: A list of games for a season
A group of linked stations carrying the same program
check.why: A network links stations by line so that they all carry the same program at once.

check.q: Which game is often named as the first coast-to-coast sports broadcast?
check.why: NBC carried the Rose Bowl from Pasadena on January 1, 1927, across the country.

check.q: What did Graham McNamee's fame show?
choices: The announcer's voice became part of what was sold
Sponsors refused to pay for sports
check.why: McNamee became a star himself, so his voice helped sell the broadcast to sponsors.

lessons.title: The First Televised Games, 1939
lessons.mainIdea: In 1939 the first televised baseball games reached only a small number of sets in the New York area.
reading: On May 17, 1939, an experimental NBC station called W2XBS showed a college baseball game between Princeton and Columbia in New York. Bill Stern described the game. There was a single camera, set on the third-base side. It could not follow a fly ball, so viewers often saw the players but not the ball.

On August 26, 1939, the same station showed a major league game for the first time. The Cincinnati Reds played the Brooklyn Dodgers at Ebbets Field. Red Barber called the game and read commercials on camera. The station used two cameras this time, one near home plate and one high in the upper deck.

Only a small number of homes around New York had a *television* set in 1939. The Second World War then slowed television's growth, because factories turned to war work. Regular *telecasts* of sports spread in the late 1940s, once sets came back into stores.

words.d: a system that sends moving pictures and sound through the air to a receiver
a program sent out by television
an early station licensed to test new broadcasting equipment

look.title: One Camera on Third Base
look.text: Princeton, 1939. A batter hits a high fly ball. The camera on the third-base side stays still. On the small screen at home, viewers see the batter drop his bat and run. The ball is gone from the picture. A few seconds later, the announcer says the ball was caught.
look.prompt: What could a radio listener learn from this play that a 1939 television viewer could not see?

check.q: What was shown on television on May 17, 1939?
check.why: W2XBS showed Princeton against Columbia, the first televised baseball game.

check.q: Which two teams played in the first televised major league game?
check.why: The Cincinnati Reds played the Brooklyn Dodgers at Ebbets Field on August 26, 1939.

check.q: Why did television grow slowly in the early 1940s?
choices: Factories turned to war work during the Second World War
check.why: The Second World War moved factories to war work, so few sets were made.

lessons.title: Sets in American Homes
lessons.mainIdea: Between 1950 and 1960, television went from a few American homes to almost all of them.
reading: The World Series was first shown on television in 1947, when the Yankees played the Dodgers. Many people watched in bars and store windows, because few families owned a set. In Chicago, WGN-TV began showing Cubs games in 1948, with Jack Brickhouse as its best-known voice for decades.

Through the 1950s, sets became cheaper and stations opened in city after city. A family's *living room* became a place where a whole season could be watched. Games that had once been heard as voices were now seen as pictures, framed by where the cameras stood.

Owners argued about television the same way they had argued about radio. Some minor league clubs lost fans when major league games reached their towns on television. The number of minor leagues fell sharply in the 1950s. Historians point to several causes, including television, the move of families to suburbs and new forms of entertainment.

words.d: the main shared room of a home, where families gathered around the television set
a lower level of professional baseball that trains players for the major leagues
a Chicago television station that began showing Cubs games in 1948

look.title: American Homes with a Television
look.cite: Nielsen Media Research household estimates, as reported by the Television Bureau of Advertising
look.prompt: In which five-year span did the share of homes with a set grow the most? What might that mean for teams deciding whether to allow telecasts?

check.q: When was the World Series first shown on television?
check.why: The 1947 Yankees–Dodgers World Series was the first on television.

check.q: About what share of U.S. homes had a television set in 1950?
check.why: Estimates put homes with a set at about 9 percent in 1950, rising to 87 percent by 1960.

check.q: Which is one cause historians give for the fall in minor leagues in the 1950s?
choices: A federal ban on minor league games
Major league games on television reaching minor league towns
check.why: Telecasts of major league games drew fans away, along with suburbs and new entertainment.

lessons.title: A League Sells as One, 1961
lessons.mainIdea: The Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961 let professional leagues sell television rights as a group.
reading: In the 1950s each National Football League team sold its own television rights. Big-city teams earned much more than small-city teams. Pete Rozelle, the NFL commissioner from 1960, wanted the league to sell all its games in one package and share the money equally.

In 1961 the league signed such a deal with CBS. A federal judge blocked it, ruling that it broke *antitrust law*, the laws against businesses joining together to limit competition. Rozelle and the leagues asked Congress for help. Congress passed the *Sports Broadcasting Act*, and President John F. Kennedy signed it on September 30, 1961.

The act allowed football, baseball, basketball and hockey leagues to *pool* their rights and sell them together. It did not cover college football. The act also let a league black out a telecast near a home game. In 1973 Congress added a rule that NFL home games sold out 72 hours ahead could not be blacked out locally.

words.d: laws that stop businesses from joining together to limit competition or fix prices
a 1961 federal law letting professional leagues sell television rights as a group
to put things together and share them, such as teams joining their television rights
a rule keeping a game off local television, often to protect ticket sales

look.title: The Law's Main Idea
look.text: The antitrust laws shall not apply to an agreement by which teams in a professional football, baseball, basketball or hockey league sell or transfer their rights in the sponsored telecasting of their games as a group.
look.cite: Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961, Public Law 87-331 (15 U.S.C. 1291)
look.prompt: Which four sports does the law name? Why would a league need Congress to say this rather than just signing a deal?

check.q: Why did a judge block the NFL's first league-wide CBS deal in 1961?
choices: It ruled that the deal broke antitrust law
check.why: The judge found that teams selling together broke the antitrust laws.

check.q: Who signed the Sports Broadcasting Act?
check.why: President Kennedy signed the act on September 30, 1961.

check.q: What did the 1973 blackout rule require?
choices: All college games must be on television
NFL home games sold out 72 hours ahead could be shown locally
Every team must sell its own rights
Radio could not carry NFL games
check.why: Congress barred local blackouts of NFL home games that sold out 72 hours before kickoff.

lessons.title: Sport in Prime Time
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1960s and 1970s, networks built weekly shows and evening games that made sport a regular part of television.
reading: On April 29, 1961, ABC began a Saturday program called Wide World of Sports. Producer Roone Arledge sent crews to events many Americans had never seen, from ski jumping to rodeo. The show used close-up cameras and personal stories to hold viewers who did not already follow a sport.

The first championship game between the NFL and the rival American Football League was played on January 15, 1967, in Los Angeles. It was later called Super Bowl I. Both CBS and NBC showed it, because each network held rights to one of the two leagues. The two leagues fully merged in 1970.

On September 21, 1970, ABC began Monday Night Football. Evening hours are called *prime time*, when the most people watch television. A game in prime time had to compete with comedies and dramas for the same audience. Arledge added more cameras and three announcers to make the game feel like an event.

words.d: the evening hours when the most people watch television
the joining of two organizations into one, such as two leagues
the person who plans and runs a television program

look.title: Two Channels, One Game
look.text: January 15, 1967. A family in Illinois turns on the television. On one channel, CBS shows the first NFL–AFL championship game. On another, NBC shows the very same game with different announcers. Each network had rights to one league.
look.prompt: Why did two networks show one game? What does that tell you about who owned the right to show a game?

check.q: Which program did ABC begin on April 29, 1961?
check.why: Roone Arledge's Wide World of Sports began on ABC in 1961.

check.q: Why did CBS and NBC both show the first Super Bowl?
choices: Each held rights to one of the two leagues
One network showed only the halftime
check.why: CBS held NFL rights and NBC held AFL rights, so both showed the game.

check.q: What does prime time mean?
choices: The first minute of a game
The evening hours when the most people watch
check.why: Prime time is the evening block with the largest television audience.

lessons.title: Instant Replay, 1963
lessons.mainIdea: In 1963 a CBS director replayed a touchdown seconds after it happened, the first instant replay on live American television.
reading: On December 7, 1963, CBS showed the Army–Navy football game from Philadelphia. The director, Tony Verna, had a heavy *videotape* machine in the truck. Videotape recorded pictures on magnetic tape that could be played back at once, unlike film, which had to be developed.

When Army quarterback Rollie Stichweh ran for a touchdown, Verna played the tape back seconds later. Announcer Lindsey Nelson warned viewers that this was not live and that Army had not scored again. This was the first *instant replay* in a live American sports telecast.

Within a few years, networks added slow-motion replays and replays from several camera angles. Replay changed how viewers judged a play. A moment that once passed in a second could now be watched again and again. A replayed moment became a *highlight*, a short piece that could be shown after the game was over.

words.d: magnetic tape that records moving pictures and sound and can be played back right away
a recording of a play shown again seconds after it happens
a short recorded piece of a game chosen to show again

look.title: The Announcer's Warning
look.text: Lindsey Nelson told viewers that what they were seeing was a replay, not a new play, and that Army had not scored a second time.
look.cite: CBS telecast of the Army–Navy game, December 7, 1963, as described by director Tony Verna
look.prompt: Why did the announcer need to explain the replay? What does this tell you about how new the idea was?

check.q: Which game had the first instant replay on live American television?
check.why: Tony Verna replayed an Army touchdown during the December 7, 1963, telecast.

check.q: How was videotape different from film?
choices: It could only show still pictures
It could be played back at once without developing
check.why: Videotape could be replayed immediately, while film had to be developed first.

check.q: What is a highlight?
choices: The brightest light in a stadium
A short recorded piece of a game chosen to show again
check.why: A highlight is a short piece of a game shown again after it happens.

lessons.title: ESPN and the Highlight Show
lessons.mainIdea: ESPN began in 1979 as an all-sports cable channel, and its SportsCenter made highlights a daily habit.
reading: *Cable television* sends programs through wires to homes that pay for a service, instead of through the air. By the late 1970s, satellites let a cable channel reach systems across the country. Bill Rasmussen and his son Scott started a channel to show sports from Connecticut and beyond.

The Entertainment and Sports Programming Network, ESPN, went on the air on September 7, 1979, from Bristol, Connecticut. Its first program was SportsCenter, a news show made of scores and highlights. Early ESPN filled many hours with events networks did not carry, such as college games and smaller sports.

SportsCenter showed dozens of games in one hour, each cut to its best seconds. Fans could now see a game's biggest moments without watching the game. Historians of media point out that this made the highlight, not the full game, the way many people came to know a season. The *twenty-four-hour* channel always needed new clips to fill time.

words.d: television sent through wires to homes that pay for the service
a machine in orbit that relays signals across long distances
running all day and night without stopping

look.title: One Hour, Many Games
look.text: A SportsCenter broadcast shows fourteen games in one hour. Each gets about three minutes, and most of that time goes to scoring plays. A baseball game that lasted three hours appears as two home runs and a final catch.
look.prompt: What kind of play gets chosen for the clip, and what kind is left out? How might that shape what a viewer thinks decided the game?

check.q: When and where did ESPN go on the air?
check.why: ESPN began broadcasting on September 7, 1979, from Bristol, Connecticut.

check.q: What was ESPN's first program?
check.why: SportsCenter, a show of scores and highlights, was ESPN's first program.

check.q: What let a cable channel reach systems across the country by the late 1970s?
check.why: Satellites relayed the channel's signal to cable systems nationwide.

lessons.title: Replay Becomes a Referee
lessons.mainIdea: Leagues began using television replay to review officials' calls, so the clip became part of the rule book.
reading: At first, replay was only for viewers at home. Officials on the field could not use it. That changed as fans saw close calls again and again and argued that the officials had been wrong. Leagues began writing *replay review* into their rules, letting an official check a recording before a call became final.

The National Football League first used replay review in 1986. It dropped the system after the 1991 season, partly because reviews made games longer. The league brought back a new version in 1999, in which coaches could *challenge* a call. The National Basketball Association began reviewing some last-second shots in 2002.

Major League Baseball was slower. It began reviewing disputed home run calls in August 2008. In 2014 it widened review to many more kinds of plays and gave managers challenges. Each league had to decide which calls a camera could judge and which stayed with the human official.

words.d: a rule letting officials check a recording before a call becomes final
a coach's or manager's formal request to have a call reviewed
a referee or umpire who enforces a game's rules

look.title: First Season of Replay Review
look.cite: League records of the NFL, NBA and Major League Baseball
look.prompt: How many years passed between the first instant replay on television in 1963 and the first league to use it for calls?

check.q: Which league first used replay review, in 1986?
check.why: The NFL first used replay review in 1986, dropped it after 1991 and brought it back in 1999.

check.q: What did Major League Baseball first review in 2008?
check.why: Baseball began with home run calls in 2008 and widened review in 2014.

check.q: Why did the NFL drop replay review after the 1991 season?
check.why: Longer games were one of the reasons the league dropped its first system.

review.q: What did radio re-creations use as their source?
review.why: Announcers rebuilt games from short telegraph messages sent from the ballpark.

review.q: Which station carried a major league game on radio on August 5, 1921?
review.why: KDKA in Pittsburgh carried the Pirates–Phillies game with Harold Arlin.

review.q: How did Cubs owner William Wrigley Jr. differ from the New York clubs of 1934–1938?
choices: He banned radio while they allowed it
He charged high fees while they gave rights away
He let stations carry games while they kept home games off the air
review.why: Wrigley opened the airwaves, while the New York clubs kept a radio ban until 1939.

review.q: What did the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961 allow?
choices: Leagues to sell television rights as a group
review.why: The act exempted pooled league television deals from antitrust law; it did not cover college football.

chapters.title: A Record Is an Argument
chapters.bigQuestion: When is a sports record a fair comparison across time, and who decides which marks count?

story.title: Sixty-One in a Longer Season
story.kicker: In 1961 two men chased one number, and the commissioner ruled that the calendar mattered.
paragraphs: It is the summer of 1961. Two New York Yankees, Roger Maris and Mickey Mantle, are hitting home runs faster than anyone since Babe Ruth. Ruth hit 60 home runs in 1927. For more than thirty years, 60 has been the most famous number in American sport.

There is a new fact in 1961. The American League has added two teams and lengthened its schedule from 154 games to 162. On July 17, Commissioner Ford Frick makes a ruling. A player who passes Ruth after his team's 154th game, he says, will be listed separately, with a mark showing the longer season.

Mantle is hurt late in the season and finishes with 54. Maris hits his 61st home run on October 1, the last day of the season, in the team's 162nd game. By Frick's ruling, record books now list two single-season marks: Ruth's 60 in 154 games and Maris's 61 in 162.

Frick never used an actual asterisk, though people remember one. The two listings last for thirty years. In 1991 a committee on records under Commissioner Fay Vincent decides that Maris alone holds the record. Maris had died in 1985. The afternoon of October 1, 1961, had been written down two different ways.
story.think: Was Frick right that a longer season made the two home run totals different kinds of records? What would you need to know to decide?

lessons.title: Hand Clocks and Electric Clocks
lessons.mainIdea: A time counts as a record only if it is measured in an approved way, and the approved way changed in 1977.
reading: The International Amateur Athletic Federation, the IAAF, was founded in 1912. One of its first jobs was to *ratify* world records, which means to check and officially approve them. A record needed a certified track, approved officials and approved timing. The body was renamed World Athletics in 2019.

For decades, officials timed races by *hand* with stopwatches, pressing a button when they saw the starter's smoke and again when a runner reached the line. Human reaction time made hand times slightly fast, and they were rounded to tenths of a second. Several timers stood at the line, and officials compared their watches.

*Fully automatic timing* starts the clock from the starter's gun and stops it from a photo at the finish line. It measures in hundredths of a second. Beginning in 1977, the IAAF accepted only fully automatic times for world records in sprint races. A hand time and an electric time for the same run are not the same number, so old and new sprint marks cannot be compared evenly.

words.d: to check and officially approve, as a governing body does with a record
timing by a person pressing a stopwatch, rounded to tenths of a second
timing started by the gun and stopped by a finish-line photo, measured to hundredths
the International Amateur Athletic Federation, founded 1912, which approves track and field records; now World Athletics

check.why: Starting in 1977, sprint records needed fully automatic timing in hundredths.

choices: Human reaction time at the start and finish

lessons.title: The Wind Gauge
lessons.mainIdea: A strong tailwind can push a sprinter or jumper, so marks set with too much wind do not count as records.
reading: A *tailwind* is wind blowing from behind, in the direction an athlete is moving. In races up to 200 meters and in the long jump and triple jump, it can help. Track rules therefore place a *wind gauge*, a device that measures wind speed, beside the track or runway.

If the tailwind is above 2.0 meters per second, a mark can still win the race, but it cannot count as a record. Record lists call it *wind-aided*. The limit of 2.0 meters per second is about 4.5 miles per hour, a light breeze to a person standing still.

The rule itself has caused arguments. At the 1988 U.S. Olympic Trials in Indianapolis, Florence Griffith Joyner ran the 100 meters in 10.49 seconds. The gauge for her race read zero, while gauges for nearby events showed strong wind. Some researchers argued the gauge was faulty. The record was ratified and still stood decades later.

words.d: wind blowing from behind, in the same direction an athlete moves
a device beside a track or runway that measures wind speed during an event
a mark set with a tailwind above the allowed limit, so it cannot be a record

lessons.title: Two Totals for Ty Cobb
lessons.mainIdea: Researchers found an error in Ty Cobb's hit total, and baseball chose to keep the old number, so books disagree.
reading: Ty Cobb played in the major leagues from 1905 to 1928, mostly for the Detroit Tigers. For decades his career hit total was listed as 4,191, the most in history. In 1985 Pete Rose passed that number, and the chase made the exact total front-page news.

Before then, researchers checking old box scores found a problem. One 1910 Detroit game appeared to have been counted twice in Cobb's totals. Without the extra game, Cobb had 4,189 hits. The Sporting News published the finding around 1981. A *box score* is the printed table of each player's results in one game.

Commissioner Bowie Kuhn's office decided not to change the *official record*. Major League Baseball kept 4,191, while some research-based books list 4,189. The dispute shows that a record is only as good as the paper behind it, and that the body with authority decides which paper counts.

words.d: a printed table listing each player's results in one game
the numbers a governing body formally accepts as true
a person who checks old sources to find and correct facts

lessons.title: Mexico City, 1968
lessons.mainIdea: The 1968 Olympics were held at high altitude, and thin air helped short races and jumps while it slowed long races.
reading: Mexico City sits about 2,240 meters, more than 7,300 feet, above sea level. It hosted the Summer Olympics in October 1968. At that *altitude* the air is thinner. Thin air pushes back less on a moving body, which helps sprinters and jumpers, but it holds less oxygen, which slows distance runners.

On October 18, 1968, Bob Beamon of the United States long jumped 8.90 meters. The old world record was 8.35, so he beat it by 55 centimeters, a jump far larger than any earlier record gain. His mark stood for almost 23 years, until Mike Powell jumped 8.95 meters in Tokyo on August 30, 1991.

Other records fell at those Games too. Jim Hines ran the 100 meters in 9.95 seconds, and Lee Evans ran the 400 meters in 43.86. Many experts linked the marks to *altitude*, and record lists began to note high-altitude marks. Distance races were slower, and runners who lived and trained at altitude, from Kenya and Ethiopia, did well.

the gas in air that the body needs; there is less of it in each breath at high altitude
the best mark ever ratified for an event by its world governing body

lessons.title: A New Javelin, 1986
lessons.mainIdea: After a javelin throw of over 104 meters in 1984, the IAAF redesigned the implement and started the records over.
reading: On July 20, 1984, East German thrower Uwe Hohn threw the javelin 104.80 meters in East Berlin. That is longer than a football field. Officials worried that throws were becoming long enough to land beyond the infield and endanger people. Javelins were also often landing flat, which made marks hard to judge.

The IAAF changed the *implement*, the object thrown. For men, the new javelin, used from 1986, moved its *center of gravity*, the balance point, 4 centimeters toward the tip. The new design came down sooner and landed point first. The women's javelin was changed in the same way in 1999.

Because the object changed, old marks could not fairly be compared with new ones. The IAAF started a new record list for the new javelin. Hohn's 104.80 meters remains a mark from a different *specification*, a written set of measurements that defines the equipment. The event kept its name, but its record book began again.

words.d: an object thrown in a track and field event, such as a javelin, shot or discus
the point where an object balances
a written set of measurements that defines what equipment must be

lessons.title: The Swimsuits of 2008 and 2009
lessons.mainIdea: New full-body swimsuits helped swimmers break dozens of records, and FINA banned them from 2010.
reading: In 2008 swimsuit makers released full-body suits with panels of *polyurethane*, a plastic material. The best known was Speedo's LZR Racer. The suits squeezed the body and trapped air, which helped swimmers float and slide through water. At the 2008 Beijing Olympics, swimmers set many world records, most of them in the new suits.

Makers then built suits made entirely of polyurethane and neoprene. At the 2009 World Championships in Rome, swimmers broke dozens of world records in a single week. Critics said the sport was measuring suits, not swimmers. The debate was called *technological doping*, a phrase comparing gear to banned drugs.

FINA, the world governing body for swimming, changed its rules. From January 1, 2010, suits had to be made of *textile*, woven cloth, and could not cover the whole body. Many records set in 2008 and 2009 stood for years afterward. Swimmers after 2010 had to chase marks set in gear they were no longer allowed to wear.

words.d: a plastic material used in the full-body swimsuits of 2008 and 2009
a critics' term for equipment that gives an unfair edge, compared to banned drugs
woven cloth
the world governing body for swimming; renamed World Aquatics in 2022

lessons.title: The IOC Begins Testing
lessons.mainIdea: After deaths and scandals linked to drugs, the IOC formed a Medical Commission in 1967 and began testing at the 1968 Games.
reading: *Doping* means using banned drugs or methods to improve performance. Stimulants such as amphetamines were used in cycling and other sports by the mid-1900s. On July 13, 1967, British cyclist Tom Simpson collapsed and died climbing Mont Ventoux during the Tour de France. Amphetamines were found in his body and in his clothing.

The International Olympic Committee formed a *Medical Commission* in 1967. At the 1968 Winter and Summer Games, it tested athletes for banned substances for the first time. At the Mexico City Games, Swedish pentathlete Hans-Gunnar Liljenwall was disqualified after a test found alcohol, which was on the banned list for shooting. His team lost its bronze medal.

Early tests could find only some drugs. Anabolic *steroids*, drugs that build muscle, were added to the IOC's banned list in the mid-1970s, once a reliable test existed. From the start, the rule makers were a step behind the drug makers. That gap has shaped arguments about which records to trust.

words.d: using banned drugs or methods to improve athletic performance
the IOC body formed in 1967 to set drug rules and run tests
here, anabolic steroids: drugs that build muscle, banned by the IOC from the mid-1970s

lessons.title: Seoul, 1988, and a World Agency
lessons.mainIdea: Ben Johnson lost his 1988 Olympic gold for steroid use, and later scandals led to the World Anti-Doping Agency in 1999.
reading: On September 24, 1988, Canadian sprinter Ben Johnson won the Olympic 100 meters in Seoul in 9.79 seconds, a world record. Three days later the IOC announced that his test had found stanozolol, an anabolic steroid. He was *stripped* of the gold medal, and the record was erased. Carl Lewis of the United States received the gold.

Canada held a public inquiry led by Justice Charles Dubin, which reported in 1990. Johnson testified that he had used steroids for years. The inquiry found that drug use was widespread in the sport. The IAAF later also removed a 1987 world record Johnson had set, after his own testimony.

In 1998 police found banned drugs with a cycling team, Festina, during the Tour de France. The IOC called a world conference, and the *World Anti-Doping Agency*, WADA, was founded on November 10, 1999. Its World Anti-Doping Code, first in force in 2004, gave most sports one shared list of banned substances and one set of *sanctions*.

words.d: officially made to give up a medal, title or record
WADA, the international body founded in 1999 to set shared anti-doping rules
a penalty, such as a ban from competition
an official public investigation

lessons.title: Records from a State Program
lessons.mainIdea: Files opened after 1990 showed East Germany ran a secret state doping program, which raised doubts about records from that era.
reading: East Germany, the German Democratic Republic, won many Olympic medals in the 1970s and 1980s for a country of about 17 million people. After Germany reunited in 1990, researchers read files of the Stasi, the East German secret police. They found records of a state *program* that gave athletes steroids, often without telling them.

The researchers Brigitte Berendonk and Werner Franke published these findings in the 1990s. The files named a secret plan known as State Plan 14.25. Many of the athletes were teenagers. In 2000 German courts convicted former sports officials and doctors for harming athletes' health.

Few East German athletes failed a test during their careers, because the program also tested athletes before they left the country. Some world records from that era still stood decades later. Governing bodies generally do not erase a record without a positive test or a confession. So the argument over those marks rests on *documents* rather than on test results.

words.d: an organized plan run by an institution; here, a secret state plan to give athletes drugs
the secret police of East Germany, whose files were opened after 1990
written records, such as files and reports, used as evidence

lessons.title: Women and the Long Races
lessons.mainIdea: For decades women were kept out of long Olympic races, so the record books for those events started late.
reading: Women first ran the 800 meters at the Olympics in Amsterdam in 1928. Newspapers reported that runners were exhausted at the finish, and some officials used the reports to argue the distance was too hard for women. The event was dropped. Women did not run an Olympic race longer than 200 meters again until the 800 meters returned in 1960 in Rome.

The Boston Marathon did not accept women. In 1966 Roberta Gibb ran it without an official number. In 1967 Kathrine Switzer entered as "K. V. Switzer" and received a number, and an official tried to pull her from the course. The race officially opened to women in 1972.

The first Olympic women's marathon was held in Los Angeles in 1984, and Joan Benoit of the United States won. Longer track races came later still. When a women's event was *excluded*, there was no official record to break. The *record book* for those events measures only the years when women were allowed to start.

an official list of the best marks ever set in each event

lessons.title: Negro Leagues Numbers Enter the Record
lessons.mainIdea: In 2020 Major League Baseball recognized seven Negro Leagues as major leagues, and in 2024 their statistics entered its records.
reading: Black players were kept out of the American and National Leagues until Jackie Robinson joined the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1947. For decades, official baseball *statistics*, the counted numbers of a player's results, left out the Negro Leagues entirely. Their greatest players had no place in the record book.

On December 16, 2020, Major League Baseball announced that it would recognize seven Negro Leagues that played from 1920 to 1948 as *major leagues*. The first of them, the Negro National League, was founded in Kansas City in 1920 under Rube Foster, who ran the Chicago American Giants. Researchers had spent years gathering box scores from Black newspapers to rebuild the numbers.

In May 2024, MLB added those statistics to its official records. Josh Gibson, a catcher for the Homestead Grays and Pittsburgh Crawfords, became the career leader in batting average at .372, ahead of Ty Cobb. Negro Leagues seasons were shorter, and many box scores are *incomplete*. Critics and supporters alike agree the record now counts players it once excluded.

the top level of professional baseball, whose numbers form the official record
